Oddtoe's prop fabrication services take a reference or a rough sketch and build the physical object — foam, resin, 3D-printed or hand-finished — ready for camera, stage or an event floor. One workshop handles the design, the build and the finish, so you brief once and collect a finished piece.

What does a prop fabrication service actually do?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

A prop fabrication service turns a brief into a built object: it designs the piece, chooses the materials and build method, and finishes it to the standard the job needs. Oddtoe runs that whole path in one workshop, so you are not coordinating a sculptor, a painter and a rigger separately.

Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="80" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="80" screen_tablet_spacer_size="80" screen_mobile_spacer_size="80"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="The question behind the question" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

What actually changes the cost of a build?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Four things: scale, how much original design the piece needs versus working from a known reference, the finish standard it has to hold up to, and whether you need one piece or several identical units.

Scale is the obvious one, but handling frequency matters just as much. A small hero prop that has to survive a close-up camera shot can take longer than a large background piece nobody examines closely, because the finish has to hold up under scrutiny.

Original design adds time before the build even starts. Working from a tight reference — a photo, a drawing, an existing product — is faster than inventing a form from a paragraph of description, because there is less to resolve before cutting begins.

Quantity changes the method as much as the hours. A single piece gets sculpted or 3D-printed directly; a run of ten identical props usually gets a mould made first, which costs more upfront and less per unit. Oddtoe scopes the build and the timeline once it has seen the brief, rather than quoting a generic day rate — send the brief and a real person answers.

Questions & Answers

prop fabrication services

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_accordion style="style-3" active_section="1" font_size="18" tab_title_google_fonts="yes" tab_title_custom_fonts="font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal" icon_size="14"][vc_tta_section title="What is prop fabrication?" tab_id="1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

Prop fabrication is turning a reference, sketch or brief into a physical object built to spec — carved foam, 3D print, cast resin or hand-finished timber, depending on what the piece needs to do. It covers the design, build and finish in one workshop, not just the making.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What materials do you fabricate props from?" tab_id="1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

Whatever the piece calls for: EVA foam and Sintra for anything worn or carried, 3D printing for repeatable or highly detailed parts, mould and cast resin for hero pieces that need to survive handling, and timber or steel where a prop has to bear real weight.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How long does prop fabrication take?" tab_id="1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

It depends on the complexity, the finish and how many are needed. A single hero piece and a run of ten identical units are different jobs even at the same size. Oddtoe scopes a build timeline once the brief and reference material are in, rather than quoting a generic turnaround.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Do you fabricate for theatre, film and events, or just one?" tab_id="1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

All three, plus brand and gallery work. The build process is the same whether the piece is walking on stage, appearing on camera, or standing on an event floor — what changes is the finish standard and how much the prop needs to withstand repeat use.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Where can I see examples of finished props?" tab_id="1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0"][vc_column_text css=""]

The studio's prop design and making page carries the finished portfolio and introduces the people doing the making.

What can a prop fabrication service build?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Anything a production, event or campaign needs to hold, wear, carry or stand next to — from a hand prop the size of a coffee cup to an oversized piece built to be photographed against. Hero pieces, background dressing and functional builds that need to open, light up or move all go through the same workshop.

Fabrication is one half of the job; knowing what to build is the other. Oddtoe's prop design and making page carries the finished portfolio and introduces the people doing the making — worth a look before you brief, so you can point at the piece closest to what you need.

An oversized fabricated piece also does double duty as an activation moment — see the brand activation ideas page for how a well-built prop earns its own photo queue at an event.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="full_width_content_paddings" el_id="pat-section-2"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="How a build gets scoped" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

How does a prop fabrication brief turn into a build plan?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Reference material and intended use come first, then material and method get chosen to fit the budget and the timeline, then the build is scheduled against the delivery date — not the other way around.

Method follows brief, not the reverse. A piece that only needs to look right in one photograph can be built faster and lighter than one that has to be handled every night of a season. Deciding the method before the use case is how budgets blow out on props that were over-built for their actual job.

The delivery date also decides the method. 3D printing suits a tight turnaround on a detailed small piece; hand carving and casting suit a hero piece with weeks to spare. Scoping the build against the date, before committing to a technique, is what keeps a fabrication project on schedule.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1691550358421{background-color: #26161f !important;}" el_id="pat-article-1"][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="4/6"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="Where the build actually starts" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

Inside a prop fabrication brief

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="19"][vc_column_text css=""]

I ask for the reference and the use case before anything else. A photo, a drawing, a description of the world the piece lives in — and how it will actually be used on the day. Something handled every performance is a different build to something that sits in a single wide shot, even if they look identical in a sketch.

From there the material choice does most of the work. Foam and Sintra carve fast and suit anything worn or carried. 3D printing is the right call for repeatable detail or a part that needs to be exact. Cast resin holds up to handling and repaints well, which matters for a hero piece that has to survive a whole season or shoot.

What surprises most first-time clients is how much of the timeline goes to finishing, well after the object is already built. A raw foam or print looks nothing like the reference until it is sealed, painted and aged to match the world it sits in. I budget real time for that stage, because a rushed finish is the fastest way to make an otherwise good build look wrong on camera.

None of this needs a technical brief. I would rather work from a bad photo of the right idea than a precise spec for the wrong one — the material and the method are my problem to solve once I understand what the piece has to do.

Foam, print or cast: how the three build methods compare

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

The same prop can be built three different ways. This is what changes between them.

CriterionFoam & Sintra3D printingMould & cast resin
Best forWorn or carried pieces, fast turnaroundRepeatable or highly detailed partsHero pieces that get handled repeatedly
TurnaroundFastestFast for one part, slower for manySlower — a mould has to be made first
Repeat unitsEach one hand-carved separatelyReprints identicallyCheap per unit once the mould exists
DurabilityLight knocks onlyDepends on the print materialHolds up to nightly handling
WeightVery lightLight to moderateHeavier, closer to the real object
Fine detailLimited by the carvingVery highHigh, and repeats exactly

Oddtoe quotes each build after a scoping conversation. Materials and finish standard decide the price.

Need it built to spec?

Prop Fabrication Services

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner el_class=”dfd_col-tablet-12″ width=”1/3″ offset=”vc_col-lg-4 vc_col-md-2 vc_col-xs-1″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner el_class=”dfd_col-tablet-12″ width=”1/3″ dfd_column_responsive_enable=”dfd-column-responsive-enable” offset=”vc_col-lg-4 vc_col-md-8 vc_col-xs-10″ css=”.vc_custom_1507277465182{padding-right: 0px !important;padding-left: 0px !important;}” responsive_styles=”padding_left_tablet:20|padding_right_tablet:20″][vc_column_text css=””]

Updated August 2026

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

Oddtoe’s prop fabrication services take a reference or a rough sketch and build the physical object — foam, resin, 3D-printed or hand-finished — ready for camera, stage or an event floor. One workshop handles the design, the build and the finish, so you brief once and collect a finished piece.

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_single_image image=”16126″ img_size=”large” alignment=”center” css=””]

The short version

What does a prop fabrication service actually do?

[vc_column_text css=””]

A prop fabrication service turns a brief into a built object: it designs the piece, chooses the materials and build method, and finishes it to the standard the job needs. Oddtoe runs that whole path in one workshop, so you are not coordinating a sculptor, a painter and a rigger separately.

Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries.

[/vc_column_text]

The question behind the question

What actually changes the cost of a build?

[vc_column_text css=””]

Four things: scale, how much original design the piece needs versus working from a known reference, the finish standard it has to hold up to, and whether you need one piece or several identical units.

Scale is the obvious one, but handling frequency matters just as much. A small hero prop that has to survive a close-up camera shot can take longer than a large background piece nobody examines closely, because the finish has to hold up under scrutiny.

Original design adds time before the build even starts. Working from a tight reference — a photo, a drawing, an existing product — is faster than inventing a form from a paragraph of description, because there is less to resolve before cutting begins.

Quantity changes the method as much as the hours. A single piece gets sculpted or 3D-printed directly; a run of ten identical props usually gets a mould made first, which costs more upfront and less per unit. Oddtoe scopes the build and the timeline once it has seen the brief, rather than quoting a generic day rate — send the brief and a real person answers.

[/vc_column_text]

Send a briefSend a brief
[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner el_class=”dfd_col-tablet-12″ width=”1/3″ offset=”vc_col-lg-4 vc_col-md-2 vc_col-xs-1″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

Questions & Answers

prop fabrication services

[/vc_column_text]

[dfd_accordion style=”style-3″ active_section=”1″ font_size=”18″ tab_title_google_fonts=”yes” tab_title_custom_fonts=”font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal” icon_size=”14″][vc_tta_section title=”What is prop fabrication?” tab_id=”1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

Prop fabrication is turning a reference, sketch or brief into a physical object built to spec — carved foam, 3D print, cast resin or hand-finished timber, depending on what the piece needs to do. It covers the design, build and finish in one workshop, not just the making.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What materials do you fabricate props from?” tab_id=”1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

Whatever the piece calls for: EVA foam and Sintra for anything worn or carried, 3D printing for repeatable or highly detailed parts, mould and cast resin for hero pieces that need to survive handling, and timber or steel where a prop has to bear real weight.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”How long does prop fabrication take?” tab_id=”1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

It depends on the complexity, the finish and how many are needed. A single hero piece and a run of ten identical units are different jobs even at the same size. Oddtoe scopes a build timeline once the brief and reference material are in, rather than quoting a generic turnaround.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Do you fabricate for theatre, film and events, or just one?” tab_id=”1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

All three, plus brand and gallery work. The build process is the same whether the piece is walking on stage, appearing on camera, or standing on an event floor — what changes is the finish standard and how much the prop needs to withstand repeat use.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Where can I see examples of finished props?” tab_id=”1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0″][vc_column_text css=””]

The studio’s prop design and making page carries the finished portfolio and introduces the people doing the making.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][/dfd_accordion][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]

What actually gets built

What can a prop fabrication service build?

[vc_column_text css=””]

Anything a production, event or campaign needs to hold, wear, carry or stand next to — from a hand prop the size of a coffee cup to an oversized piece built to be photographed against. Hero pieces, background dressing and functional builds that need to open, light up or move all go through the same workshop.

Fabrication is one half of the job; knowing what to build is the other. Oddtoe’s prop design and making page carries the finished portfolio and introduces the people doing the making — worth a look before you brief, so you can point at the piece closest to what you need.

An oversized fabricated piece also does double duty as an activation moment — see the brand activation ideas page for how a well-built prop earns its own photo queue at an event.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]

[vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”full_width_content_paddings” el_id=”pat-section-2″][vc_column]
[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″]

How a build gets scoped

How does a prop fabrication brief turn into a build plan?

[vc_column_text css=””]

Reference material and intended use come first, then material and method get chosen to fit the budget and the timeline, then the build is scheduled against the delivery date — not the other way around.

Method follows brief, not the reverse. A piece that only needs to look right in one photograph can be built faster and lighter than one that has to be handled every night of a season. Deciding the method before the use case is how budgets blow out on props that were over-built for their actual job.

The delivery date also decides the method. 3D printing suits a tight turnaround on a detailed small piece; hand carving and casting suit a hero piece with weeks to spare. Scoping the build against the date, before committing to a technique, is what keeps a fabrication project on schedule.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row]
[vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1691550358421{background-color: #26161f !important;}” el_id=”pat-article-1″][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”4/6″]

Where the build actually starts

Inside a prop fabrication brief

[vc_column_text css=””]

I ask for the reference and the use case before anything else. A photo, a drawing, a description of the world the piece lives in — and how it will actually be used on the day. Something handled every performance is a different build to something that sits in a single wide shot, even if they look identical in a sketch.

From there the material choice does most of the work. Foam and Sintra carve fast and suit anything worn or carried. 3D printing is the right call for repeatable detail or a part that needs to be exact. Cast resin holds up to handling and repaints well, which matters for a hero piece that has to survive a whole season or shoot.

What surprises most first-time clients is how much of the timeline goes to finishing, well after the object is already built. A raw foam or print looks nothing like the reference until it is sealed, painted and aged to match the world it sits in. I budget real time for that stage, because a rushed finish is the fastest way to make an otherwise good build look wrong on camera.

None of this needs a technical brief. I would rather work from a bad photo of the right idea than a precise spec for the wrong one — the material and the method are my problem to solve once I understand what the piece has to do.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]

Which build method fits your prop?

Foam, print or cast: how the three build methods compare

[vc_column_text css=””]

The same prop can be built three different ways. This is what changes between them.

Criterion Foam & Sintra 3D printing Mould & cast resin
Best for Worn or carried pieces, fast turnaround Repeatable or highly detailed parts Hero pieces that get handled repeatedly
Turnaround Fastest Fast for one part, slower for many Slower — a mould has to be made first
Repeat units Each one hand-carved separately Reprints identically Cheap per unit once the mould exists
Durability Light knocks only Depends on the print material Holds up to nightly handling
Weight Very light Light to moderate Heavier, closer to the real object
Fine detail Limited by the carving Very high High, and repeats exactly

How to brief a prop fabrication project

[vc_column_text css=””]

Send reference images first, even rough ones. A photo of something close to what you want, or a sketch on a napkin, tells me more than a paragraph of adjectives. Say what the piece is for and where it will be seen — camera, stage, or an event floor — because that decides the finish standard before the design even starts.

Tell me how it gets used. Something picked up and set down once is a different build to something carried through a full run of performances. Say how many are needed too — one hero piece and a set of ten identical units are scoped and priced differently from the first conversation.

Share whatever constraints already exist: a weight limit for something worn, a size limit for transport, a colour that has to match an existing set or costume. Constraints narrow the material choice fast and save a round of revisions later.

If you are not sure fabrication is even the right approach — sometimes an existing piece can be sourced and modified faster than one built from scratch — say that too. Send the brief through the contact page and I will tell you honestly which path suits the timeline and the budget.
